---
title: "Amines and aromaticity: where is the lone pair?"
---

Allow 60–75 minutes. Draw structures rather than relying on a nitrogen label.
You need formal charges, pKa comparisons and resonance. No metabolic knowledge
is assumed.

## 1. Classify and protonate

Draw methylamine, dimethylamine and trimethylamine with their nitrogen lone
pairs. Classify each as primary, secondary or tertiary. Protonate each once,
showing an explicit acid H–A as donor and the corresponding A⁻ product. Count
bonds and formal charge on every nitrogen before and after the change.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A neutral nitrogen with three ordinary single bonds has one lone pair. After
using that pair to bind H, it has four bonds and a positive charge.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
CH₃NH₂, (CH₃)₂NH and (CH₃)₃N have one, two and three carbon substituents on N,
respectively. Their conjugate acids are CH₃NH₃⁺, (CH₃)₂NH₂⁺ and (CH₃)₃NH⁺.
Draw N pair → H and H–A bond → A in the same proton transfer. A tertiary amine
is neutral before protonation; it is not the same as a quaternary ammonium
ion bearing four carbon substituents.
:::

## 2. Compare base strength using supplied data

Use approximate aqueous conjugate-acid pKa values: ethylammonium 10.7 and
anilinium 4.6. Which corresponding neutral amine is the stronger base? Estimate
the equilibrium constant for anilinium + ethylamine ⇌ aniline + ethylammonium.
Explain the structural difference without asserting that basicity determines
all nucleophilic reaction rates.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
Ethylamine is the stronger base because its conjugate acid is weaker (larger
pKa). The estimated constant is 10^(10.7 − 4.6), about 1.26 × 10⁶ toward
aniline and ethylammonium. Aniline can delocalise its N pair into the aromatic
ring. Basicity concerns an equilibrium; nucleophilicity concerns a reaction
rate and also depends on substrate, solvent and other factors.
:::

## 3. Count the aromatic electrons carefully

Draw benzene, cyclohexane, pyridine and pyrrole. For each state whether a
continuous cyclic pi system exists. In pyridine and pyrrole identify whether
the nitrogen lone pair contributes to the aromatic sextet. Predict which
nitrogen is more readily protonated under comparable ordinary conditions.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
Benzene has six pi electrons and is aromatic. Cyclohexane lacks continuous
conjugation and is nonaromatic. Pyridine N contributes one electron to its
pi system; its separate lone pair is available to bind a proton while retaining
aromaticity. Pyrrole uses its pair in the six-electron aromatic system, making
ordinary N protonation much less favourable. Pyridine is therefore the more
basic nitrogen in this comparison. “Both contain a ring N” misses the orbital
difference.
:::

## 4. Draw glycine across pH

Use supplied approximate pKa values 2.3 for the carboxyl group and 9.6 for
the ammonium group. Draw the dominant form at pH 1, 6 and 12; label every
formal charge and calculate the net charge. Explain what changes around each
pKa, rather than implying an abrupt switch between pure forms.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
At pH well below a site's pKa, its protonated form predominates. At pH well
above it, its deprotonated form predominates. Apply this separately to the two
sites.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
At pH 1: H₃N⁺–CH₂–COOH, net +1. At pH 6: H₃N⁺–CH₂–COO⁻, net zero. At pH
12: H₂N–CH₂–COO⁻, net −1. The middle form is a zwitterion because it contains
both positive and negative formal charges. Around each pKa adjacent forms
coexist; these drawings describe dominant forms sufficiently away from the
transition, not an all-or-nothing population rule.
:::

## 5. Amine versus peptide nitrogen

Place CH₃CH₂NH₂ and CH₃CONH₂ side by side. Draw the amide resonance
contributors and explain why assigning “amine-like basicity” to every
nitrogen in a protein would fail. Give one structural feature you would
inspect before predicting the nitrogen's behaviour.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The amide N pair is delocalised into a neighbouring carbonyl; the simple amine
pair is not. Peptide nitrogens are amide nitrogens. Inspect direct attachment
to C=O, aromaticity and conjugation before applying a simple alkylamine model.
:::
